activities.caption: file the symptoms — three ways a benchmark lies
activities.name: ebsBenchmarkBuckets

config.prompt: Shared benchmarks are systematically unfaithful to deployment. File each symptom:

items.label: models ingest the benchmark or near-duplicates — scores partly measure memorisation
frontier labs maintain private, rotating test sets
models that top MMLU flub trivially rephrased versions of its questions
adversarially rephrased benchmarks built to expose the optimisation
static, English-centric, clean inputs — while products meet typos and dialects

config.why: The professional stance: a benchmark is a finger pointing at capability — useful for comparisons and regressions, unearned as a deployment guarantee.

activities.anchor: A model is a snapshot of its training distribution
activities.caption: pair each scenario with its shift regime
activities.name: ebsShiftMatch

config.prompt: Distribution shift: the silent killer — pair each scenario with its regime:

pairs.left: a hospital replaces its scanner; image statistics change
pairs.right: covariate shift — inputs change, the underlying relationship holds

pairs.left: what counts as fraud evolves as fraudsters adapt
pairs.right: concept drift — the relationship itself changes

pairs.left: a spam filter's success changes what spam looks like
pairs.right: concept drift caused by deploying the model

pairs.left: pandemic-era demand forecasts trained on history meet a world with no history

config.why: The monitoring loop: track input and output distributions, alert on anomalies, re-evaluate periodically against freshly labelled data — because accuracy can decay for months with no error message anywhere.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the monitoring posture
activities.name: ebsGateSpot

config.prompt: This operations summary contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: A model is a snapshot of its training distribution, but the world keeps moving.
Covariate shift changes the inputs while the underlying relationship holds.
Concept drift invalidates the model — and deploying it can cause the drift.
Once the model passes evaluation and ships, the evaluating is finished.
Accuracy can decay for months with no error message anywhere.
config.correction: For deployed systems evaluation is a vital sign, not a launch gate — continuous monitoring with scheduled re-evaluation against fresh labels.
config.why: Teams that budget for perpetual evaluation ship models that decay slowly and visibly; teams that test once ship models that decay quickly and silently.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — the failure gap Gender Shades hid
activities.name: ebsGapEstimate

config.prompt: In Gender Shades, error on lighter-skinned men was at most 0.8%; on darker-skinned women it reached 34.7%. Roughly how many times larger is that failure rate?
config.why: 34.7 ÷ 0.8 ≈ 43 — a failure gap of more than 40× behind a tolerable aggregate, driven by training data skewed toward lighter and male faces.
config.context: The study's method matters as much as its result: disaggregated evaluation on a deliberately balanced probe set, before deployment, with subgroups chosen by the people who could be harmed.

activities.caption: drag the divider — one tool, two readings of fair
activities.name: ebsFairnessCompare

config.prompt: The COMPAS controversy, lens by lens:

before.label: Calibration lens
before.text: The recidivism score was calibrated across races — risk scores meant the same thing for every group.

after.label: Equal-error lens
after.text: It imposed roughly twice the false-positive burden on Black defendants as on white ones — both facts true simultaneously.

config.why: When base rates differ between groups, demographic parity, equalised odds and calibration cannot all hold at once — choosing among criteria is a policy decision for affected stakeholders and regulators.

activities.anchor: A worked example shows why base rates rule
activities.caption: which curve is the false-alarm share?
activities.name: ebsBaseRateTrace

config.prompt: A screener is 99% accurate in both directions. Which curve shows the false-alarm share of the flagged pool as the condition's prevalence (x) rises?
config.why: At 1% prevalence the flagged pool is exactly half wrong — coin-flip odds per flag; at 10% prevalence the share drops to about 8%. Identical error rates mean different things for different subpopulations — which is why the fairness criteria collide.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — safety as a process
activities.name: ebsDefenceCloze

config.text: The standing defence is %%0%% — paying people and automated suites to break your own system before release, then %%1%% after every patch: a never-converging %%2%% rather than a checklist. Adversarial examples predate LLMs: imperceptible pixel perturbations flip image classifiers.
config.hint: Test, patch, retest — with humans trying to break it the way real adversaries would.

activities.anchor: patched the way a buffer overflow can
activities.caption: ship the agent — one week of safety work
activities.name: ebsShipBranch

config.root: An LLM agent with tool access ships next week. You have one week of safety work. Where does it go?

choices.label: Instruct the model to ignore embedded instructions
Red-team: pay people and automated suites to break it before release
Ship now; patch when users report holes

instruct.text: Damage limitation at best: data and instructions share one medium — natural language — so filtering and prompt-hardening reduce success rates but never create the hard boundary the database world got from separating query language from data.

redteam.text: The standing defence: jailbreaks, prompt injection and adversarial images found before release, then re-tested after every patch — a never-converging arms race rather than a checklist.

later.text: Users and adversaries actively probe for behaviours you never tested; least-privilege tools and human confirmation for irreversible actions exist precisely because 'after users find it' is not a plan.

config.why: Safety is empirical and iterative — robust, corrigible behaviour under adversarial pressure remains an open research problem, so the engineering response is damage limitation, not the false comfort of a single fix.
